questions.prompt: Why would a person with very few helper T cells struggle to make antibodies against most protein antigens?

options.text: Without helper T cells, MHC-1 disappears from every body cell
Protein antigens need T-dependent activation, which needs helper T cells
Helper T cells are the cells that actually secrete antibodies
B cells mature in the thymus, which helper T cells control

questions.prompt: A B cell binds an antigen but is NOT activated. What does it do next in T-dependent activation?

options.text: Becomes a plasma cell immediately and starts secreting IgM
Undergoes apoptosis so it can't make a mistaken response
Displays it on MHC-2 and waits for a helper T cell to confirm it
Displays it on MHC-1 so a cytotoxic T cell can confirm it

questions.explanation: The helper T cell's interleukin then activates it.

questions.prompt: Which double binding activates a helper T cell?

options.text: CD8 binds MHC-2
Fc receptor binds IgE
TCR binds the antigen and CD4 binds MHC-2
TCR binds MHC-1 and CD8 binds the antigen
Cytotoxic T cell — CD8 — MHC-1
Cytotoxic T cell — CD4 — MHC-2
NK cell — CD4 — MHC-2
Helper T cell — CD8 — MHC-1

questions.prompt: Which statement about apoptosis is FALSE?

options.text: It spills contents that cause strong inflammation.
It can be induced by granzyme.
The membrane shows blebbing.
It is pre-programmed cell death.
The cell's genome is degraded.

questions.explanation: Apoptosis avoids inflammation; necrosis causes it.

questions.prompt: Why does a cytotoxic T cell sacrifice a virus-infected host cell?

options.text: It converts the infected cell into an antibody-making plasma cell
The infected cell will heal faster after going through apoptosis
It needs the infected cell's MHC-2 to activate other T cells
Killing it before it releases new viruses protects nearby cells

questions.explanation: Similar logic to interferon: sacrifice one to save many.

questions.prompt: Organ transplant patients take immunosuppressive drugs. Which cells would otherwise attack the transplant?

options.text: Plasma cells only, which release antibodies against the graft
Mast cells, which release histamine into the transplant
Red blood cells, which clot inside the transplanted organ
Cytotoxic T cells, which destroy cells from other people

questions.explanation: Slides list transplanted tissue as a cytotoxic T cell target.

questions.prompt: An NK cell meets a healthy liver cell displaying MHC-1. What happens?

options.text: MHC-1 binding inhibits the NK cell, so it leaves
It secretes antibodies to coat the liver cell
It turns into a cytotoxic T cell and checks MHC-1
It kills the liver cell with perforin and granzyme

questions.prompt: A patient's centrifuged blood shows an unusually thick buffy coat. What does this most likely suggest?

options.text: Anemia (too few red blood cells)
An infection (high WBC count)
AIDS (a low WBC count)
Dehydration (too little plasma)

questions.explanation: WBCs form the middle grayish layer.

questions.prompt: Why did Köhler fuse B cells with cancer cells?

options.text: To make sure every antibody produced was specific for cancer
Isolated B cells die after a few divisions; cancer cells are immortal
Cancer cells make better antibodies than B cells ever could
B cells can't make any antibodies outside the body on their own

questions.explanation: The hybridoma keeps making the antibody indefinitely.

questions.prompt: In a rapid antigen test, what makes the test line visible?

options.text: Dyed chicken antibodies bind directly to the test line
The nasal sample dries red wherever the strip is wettest
A dyed antibody–antigen complex is caught by fixed antibodies
The viral antigen itself is red and sticks to the paper

questions.explanation: The dye rides on the constant region of the conjugate antibody.

questions.prompt: A test strip shows a T line but no C line. What should you conclude?

options.text: Positive — the T line shows antigen
Negative — a T line alone means nothing
Positive, but only if repeated twice
Invalid — the test didn't run correctly

questions.prompt: Why are COVID monoclonal antibody treatments not a substitute for a vaccine?

options.text: They give passive immunity that fades and may not create memory
They are made by T cells, which can't neutralize the coronavirus
They only work in mice, the animals they were first made in
They cause allergies by triggering IgE on the patient's mast cells

questions.prompt: Describe two ways NK cells identify targets and how they kill them.
questions.explanation: Fc receptors bind the constant region of antibodies coating a target (e.g., a parasite) — antibody-dependent cytotoxicity. MHC-1 receptors detect self; cells lacking MHC-1 (e.g., some cancer cells) lose that inhibitory signal and are attacked. They kill with perforin and granzymes.

questions.prompt: Explain how monoclonal antibodies are produced.
questions.explanation: Inject an antigen into an animal (e.g., a mouse) → isolate a B cell making the desired antibody → fuse it with an immortal cancer (myeloma) cell using ethylene glycol to make a hybridoma → grow the hybridoma indefinitely and harvest its identical antibodies.
